list.listitem: Consider Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) in patients with peptic ulcer disease refractory to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), ulcers distal to the duodenal bulb, multiple peptic ulcers, or family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) 1 syndrome. C
Only patients with a family history of MEN 1 syndrome should be considered for screening, as the incidence of ZES is very low. C
Fasting hypergastrinemia with acid hypersecretion confirms the diagnosis. C
Provocative tests are helpful for diagnosis in moderate hypergastrinemia. C
PPIs are the mainstay of treatment, and an attempt should be made to remove the tumor surgically after localization with somatostatin receptor scintigraphy with endoscopic ultrasound. A
Surgical exploration and tumor removal are the recommended procedures for all patients without hepatic metastases. B

background.definition: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a rare condition characterized by peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease and sometimes diarrhea caused by marked elevation of serum gastrin.

list.listitem: 1 to 3 cases per million individuals every year.
0.1% to 1% among patients with peptic ulcer disease.
Slightly more common in men (M/F ratio 1.5-2:1.0).
Mean age of presentation 40 to 50 years but can occur at any age.
Sporadic tumors account for 75% to 80% of cases.
Twenty-five percent to 30% are associated with MEN 1 syndrome. The tumors are usually multicentric in origin.

Ninety percent of gastrinomas arise from the gastrinoma triangle, which is formed by a line joining the confluence of the cystic and common bile ducts superiorly, the junction of the second and third portion of the duodenum inferiorly, and the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas medially.

A systematic review of 7 trials with 1789 participants taking long term PPIs found an increased risk of focal or linear/micronodular enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia, but no increase in the risk of dysplastic or neoplastic change.

Elevated gastrin peptide from the tumor cells stimulates parietal cell hyperplasia in the stomach, causing prominent gastric folds and increased acid output from the parietal cells, resulting in peptic ulcer.

Diarrhea occurs in more than two-thirds of patients due to the high volume of gastric secretions, inactivation of pancreatic and intestinal enzymes by acidic pH, and direct toxic effects of acid on the intestinal epithelial cells, causing malabsorption.
No routine screening is indicated in patients without a positive family history. C
Persons diagnosed with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome should be evaluated for MEN-1 syndrome with calcium, PTH and prolactin levels.
Consider annual fasting gastrin, serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, and prolactin levels in first-degree relatives of people with MEN-1 syndrome. Discontinue screening after 45 years of age. C
Consider ZES in patients with peptic ulcer disease refractory to PPIs, ulcers distal to duodenal bulb, multiple peptic ulcers, or a family history of MEN-1 syndrome. C
Fasting hypergastrinemia greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal with acid hypersecretion (pH <4.0) confirms the diagnosis. C
Perform a secretin provocative test for diagnosis in patients who have hypergastrinemia with levels less than 10 times upper limit of normal. C
Perform a calcium provocative test in patients with strong clinical suspicion who have a negative secretin stimulation test. C
Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy with or without endoscopic ultrasound is useful to identify the location of the tumor. B

list.listitem: Suspect ZES in patients with peptic ulcer disease refractory to PPIs, peptic ulcer disease with chronic diarrhea without any other etiology, ulcer distal to first part of the duodenum, multiple peptic ulcers, recurrent ulcers after surgery, and family history of MEN-1.

Upper abdominal pain is the most common symptom; 75% of patients also experience diarrhea, while heartburn is the third most common symptom. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, GI bleeding, weight loss, and (rarely) perforated ulcer.
GI bleeding from an ulcer and jaudice is the presenting symptom in 25% of patients with an advacanced tumor.
The presence of colicky abdominal pain should raise the suspicion of nephrolithiasis in patients with MEN-1 syndrome.
Findings on physical examination can be normal. Sometimes dental erosions are seen due to gastroesophageal reflux disease.

The differential diagnosis of elevated gastrin levels is based on pH. If pH is less than 4.0, consider gastrinoma, antral gastric cell hyperplasia, and H. pylori infection. If pH is more than 4.0, consider PPI or H2 blocker use, pernicious anemia, or postvagotomy.
Fasting hypergastrinemia over 10 times the upper limit of normal with acid hypersecretion (pH <4.0 or basal acid output >15 mEq/h) confirms the diagnosis.

However, in two-thirds of patients with ZES, fasting serum gastrin levels overlap with values seen in other conditions. In these patients, gastrin provocative tests such as secretin or calcium tests are used to confirm the diagnosis.
The secretin test is more sensitive than the calcium provocation test and has fewer side effects; it should be the initial provocative test of choice.

In ZES patients with a negative secretin test, 38% to 50% have a positive calcium provocation test. Therefore, the calcium test should be considered in all patients with a strong clinical suspicion of ZES but a negative secretin test.

The use of widespread PPI has been a major concern in making a diagnosis of ZES because of the extended duration of action and the resultant hypergastrinemia in normal subjects. Some experts have suggested that the use of PPI can produce a false positive secretin stimulation test. However, in a recent retrospective analysis comparing accuracy for 29 patients taking a PPI and 70 not taking one, accuracy was non-inferior for those taking a PPI. These findings suggest that PPI withdrawal prior to secretin stimulation test may not be required.

Obtain levels of serum calcium, phosphorus, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), growth hormone, prolactin, and cortisol in all patients to identify MEN 1 syndrome. Order an MRI of the head if MEN 1 syndrome is suspected.
(Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy) is the most sensitive imaging modality for localization of primary or metastatic lesions and is superior to endoscopic ultrasound and MRI.
Endoscopic ultrasound is especially valuable for small pancreatic and duodenal tumors and can permit fine needle aspiration for histological diagnosis.
MRI or CT scan for localization of tumor are inferior to SRS and EUS. Their sensitivity is less, and, frequently, tumors smaller than 1 cm are missed.
See the diagnosis algorithm in .
PPIs in high doses are the mainstay of treatment in all patients. A
The recommended treatment for all patients without hepatic metastases is surgical exploration and tumor removal. B
Hepatic resection or hepatic artery embolization can be beneficial in patients with hepatic predominant disease. C
Surgery is usually not recommended for gastrinomas in MEN 1 syndrome syndrome due to the multifocal nature of the tumors and a relatively benign course. C

PPIs in high doses are the mainstay of medical treatment in healing peptic ulcers. Typical doses are esomeprazole 120 mg daily, pantoprazole 120 mg daily, omeprazole 60 mg daily, lansoprazole 45 mg daily, and rabeprazole 60 mg daily. PPIs at high doses will heal most of the ulcers (80%-85%), which will generally recur after stopping medications. A gradual PPI dose reduction is possible after healing, although low-dose PPIs should be continued indefinitely.
Long-term treatment with PPIs appears to be safe, without any evidence of hematologic, biochemical, or gastric toxicity.

However recent studies have shown that prolonged PPI use have been associated with intestinal dysbiosis resulting in increased risk for pneumonia intestinal infections such as Clostridium difficile infection and Small Intestine Bacterial Overgrowth(SIBO). Some studies have shown compelling evidence that the use of probiotics supplementation with PPI therapy can reduce these emerging side effects . Examples of these probiotic strains include Lactobacillus reuteri, Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Lactobacillus pentosus
IV pantoprazole can be used in critically ill patients or those who cannot tolerate oral intake.

For metastatic disease, chemotherapy and octreotide may be useful in addition to PPIs, especially in patients with MEN 1 syndrome. However, the action of octreotide is unpredictable in decreasing gastrin levels and symptoms in gastrinomas.
Surgical exploration and resection of the tumor is recommended for all patients with sporadic gastrinomas, especially if there is no evidence of liver metastases.
Preoperative localization with somatostatin receptor scintigraphy and/or endoscopic ultrasound will increase the chances of complete tumor resection.
Primary tumor resection will significantly decrease the incidence of metastases and will increase overall survival rates, although total cure is achieved in only one-third of the patients.
The presence of hepatic metastases decreases the survival rate.
Hepatic resection can be considered if the patient has a single or few metastases localized to a hepatic lobe.

There is little evidence showing that surgery is beneficial in patients with MEN 1 syndrome, since the gastrinomas are usually multifocal in origin, follow a relatively benign course, and have high 10-year survival rates.

A recent retrospective analysis of 108 patients with non-metastatic sporadic gastrinoma revealed an overall median survival rate of 173 months and a 5-year survival rate of 94% for duodenal gastrionomas . For pancreatic gastrinomas, the median survival rate was 93 months with a 5-year disease-free survival rate of 63%. Tumor size >2cm and tumor grade were independent predictors of recurrence.
The presence of hepatic metastasis is a poor prognostic indicator. B
Patients with MEN 1 syndrome usually have relative high survival rates and lower rates of hepatic metastases. B
